name: HALLIGAN, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the defendant's arrest was an unlawful "constructive entry" violating Payton and the State Constitution, and that the Appellate Division must re-evaluate the voluntariness of the third-party consent using the correct legal standard for the weapon possession charge.

name: SINGAS, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Appellate Division correctly found the tenant's consent voluntary, that attenuation analysis is not applicable to third-party consent following a Payton violation, and that the majority's new "constructive entry" rule and State Constitution analysis are unpreserved and legally unsound.

name: WILSON, Chief Judge
description: Concurred, argued that political subdivisions generally lack the capacity to challenge state laws, and Newburgh failed to meet the narrow 'dilemma' exception for facial constitutional challenges.

name: TROUTMAN, J.
description: Concurred, argued that a defendant can forfeit the constitutional right to a trial by a jury of 12 through egregious misconduct, especially when no alternate jurors are available and the misconduct affects a deliberating juror, thereby protecting the integrity of the justice system.

name: GARCIA, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Article IX of the State Constitution does not expressly or implicitly limit the legislature's plenary authority to mandate the timing of certain elections, and therefore the Even Year Election Law is a proper exercise of that authority.

name: CANNATARO, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the Climate Act does not preempt local laws regulating greenhouse gas emissions, as the State Legislature did not express or imply an intent to occupy the entire field and explicitly encouraged complementary local action.

name: RIVERA, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the Act is constitutional because New York's separation of powers doctrine is flexible, the Governor's appointment and removal powers are not exclusive, and the Act serves the paramount goal of maintaining public trust by limiting executive self-regulation in ethics enforcement.

name: Judge Garcia
description: Dissented, argued that the Act unconstitutionally encroaches on executive power by creating a commission with sweeping enforcement authority, a majority of legislative appointees, and limited executive oversight, thereby violating bedrock separation of powers principles.

name: Judge Singas
description: Concurred with Judge Garcia's dissenting opinion.

name: Judge Scarpulla
description: Concurred with Judge Garcia's dissenting opinion.

name: Judge Cannataro
description: Took no part in the decision.

name: WILSON, Chief Judge
description: Concurred, argued that the New York Constitution's Article II, Section 1 explicitly restricts voting to citizens, and home rule powers under Article IX do not permit localities to expand suffrage beyond this.

name: RIVERA, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Article II, Section 1 is an affirmative right for citizens but does not prohibit localities from enfranchising noncitizens under home rule, though Local Law 11 is void for not having a public referendum.

name: WILSON, Chief Judge
description: Concurred, argued that the New York Constitution's text does not explicitly require in-person voting, and the historical context, including the removal of a relevant provision in 1966 and the legislature's plenary power under Article II, Section 7, supports the constitutionality of the Early Mail Voter Act.

name: RIVERA, J.
description: Concurred, argued that while the Constitution historically required in-person voting, the 1966 amendment removed the Election District Provision, eliminating any express or implied constitutional limitation on the legislature's power to allow mail-in voting, and criticized the majority's historical analysis and speculation on political motives.

name: Judge Troutman
description: Concurred, argued that the Constitution as currently written does not prohibit the legislature's enactment of the challenged statute, aligning with Judge Rivera's opinion.

name: GARCIA, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the New York Constitution, particularly Article II, Section 2, explicitly limits the legislature's authority to provide absentee voting only for specific categories of voters, and the Early Mail Voter Act violates this limitation, further disregarding the will of the People who recently rejected a constitutional amendment for no-excuse absentee voting.

name: HALLIGAN, J.
description: Concurred, argued that trial counsel was not ineffective because requesting a cross-racial identification instruction was discretionary at the time, and the failure to request it was not an egregious error given the legal landscape.

name: WILSON, Chief Judge
description: Concurred, argued that the representation was constitutionally sufficient as the Boone rule was a rule of evidence, not a due process determination, and counsel did request a general expanded jury charge.

name: TROUTMAN, J.
description: Dissented, argued that trial counsel was ineffective for failing to request a cross-racial identification charge given its widespread importance at the time and the case's reliance on a single cross-racial identification.

name: RIVERA, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the importance of cross-racial identification charges was well-understood before Boone, and the majority's conclusion that the legal argument was not compelling enough is incorrect, joining Judge Troutman's dissent.

name: Wilson, Chief Judge
description: Concurred, argued that counsel's failure to request the only applicable defense instruction (voluntary surrender) despite supporting testimony constituted ineffective assistance, depriving the defendant of a fair trial.

name: CANNATARO, J.
description: Dissented, argued that counsel was not ineffective as the defendant was not entitled to a voluntary surrender instruction, and the majority's ruling ignores facts, lacks common sense, and is dangerous as a matter of policy.

name: RIVERA, J.
description: Concurred, argued that police interference with a bicyclist is a seizure requiring reasonable suspicion or probable cause, similar to a motor vehicle stop, and the officers lacked this.

name: SINGAS, J.
description: Dissented, argued that police encounters with bicyclists should be evaluated on a case-by-case basis, not a per se seizure rule, and the officers had founded suspicion.

name: Judge Halligan
description: Took no part in the decision.

name: Chief Judge Wilson
description: Concurred, argued that the 2014 constitutional amendments limit court-drawn maps to only what is necessary to remedy a violation of law, and therefore the IRC has a continuing constitutional duty to produce new maps for future elections.

name: Judge Cannataro
description: Dissented, argued that the court-ordered maps from Harkenrider should remain in force until the next federal decennial census, and the majority's decision rewrites the Constitution and undermines the judiciary's role in safeguarding fair elections.

name: GARCIA, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Administrative Code § 10-181 is a valid exercise of the City's municipal law-making authority, as it is neither preempted by state law nor unconstitutionally vague.

name: WILSON, CHIEF JUDGE
description: Concurred, argued that the legislature's grant of rulemaking authority to the Commission on Forensic Sciences was sufficient to authorize the promulgation of the Familial DNA Search Regulations.

name: LINDLEY, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the legislature did not authorize the Commission or DNA Subcommittee to make policy-laden decisions like permitting familial DNA searching, which constitutes impermissible legislative policy-making by an administrative agency.

name: WILSON, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the People's unexplained and inexplicable delay of over four years in prosecuting the case violated the defendant's constitutional right to prompt prosecution, necessitating dismissal of the indictment.

name: SINGAS, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the pre-indictment delay did not violate the defendant's due process rights, especially considering the seriousness of the crime and the lack of actual prejudice to the defendant, and that the majority's decision undermines justice for sexual assault victims.

name: GARCIA, Judge
description: Dissented, argued that the Appellate Division correctly upheld the denial of the motion to dismiss on constitutional speedy trial grounds.

name: TROUTMAN, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the warrantless inspections authorized by the ELD rule fall within the administrative search exception to the warrant requirement and do not constitute unreasonable searches and seizures under the State Constitution.

name: CANNATARO, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Local Law No. 2 is consistent with RPTL article 11 and the state constitution's home rule article, as it effectuates a power granted to cities to opt back into the state tax enforcement scheme without requiring an agreement under RPTL 1150.

name: WILSON, CHIEF JUDGE
description: Concurred, argued that the police lacked reasonable suspicion to believe Mr. Johnson had committed a crime or was in possession of a weapon, and thus the evidence seized from the unjustified stop and frisk must be suppressed.

name: RIVERA, J.
description: Concurred, argued that while agreeing with the result, the De Bour framework itself is flawed and has proven counterproductive, failing to protect individuals from subconstitutional abuses and contributing to racial profiling and dangerous escalations in police encounters.

name: Cannataro, Acting Chief Judge
description: Concurred, argued that the enabling act is a valid assignment of power to a temporary commission with adequate standards and legislative oversight, thus not an unconstitutional delegation.

name: WILSON, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the Committee acted permissibly but expressed concern that the Enabling Act weakened the Governor's ability to check legislative and executive compensation.

name: SINGAS, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Enabling Act unconstitutionally delegated core legislative power to an unelected committee, bypassing constitutional lawmaking procedures and violating the "fixed by law" requirement for salaries.

name: DiFIORE, Chief Judge
description: Concurred, argued that the legislature's redistricting maps were procedurally unconstitutional due to the IRC's failure to follow the mandated process and substantively unconstitutional due to partisan gerrymandering, requiring new maps.

name: TROUTMAN, J.
description: Dissented in part, argued that the majority's opinion on substantive gerrymandering was an inappropriate advisory opinion and that the legislature should be ordered to adopt one of the IRC-approved plans rather than having a court-appointed special master draw new maps.

name: WILSON, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the petitioners failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the 2022 redistricting maps violated the Constitution through partisan gerrymandering, and agreed with Judge Troutman's proposed remedy.

name: RIVERA, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the legislature did not violate redistricting procedures or constitutional mandates, and petitioners failed to prove unconstitutional partisan gerrymandering.

name: WILSON, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Mr. Dawson unequivocally requested counsel, and the majority's decision vitiates the privilege against self-incrimination, right to counsel, and due process.

name: Judge Rivera
description: Concurred with Judge Wilson's dissenting opinion.

name: Chief Judge DiFIORE
description: Concurred, argued that interactive fantasy sports contests are skill-based competitions, not gambling, as participants exercise substantial influence over the outcome through skill and knowledge.

name: Judge Wilson
description: Dissented, argued that interactive fantasy sports contests are gambling under the common understanding of the term in the Constitution and that the majority's decision usurps the voters' prerogative and judicial role.

name: Judge Garcia
description: Took no part in the decision.

name: GARCIA, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the Right of Way Law is constitutional and not preempted by state law, as ordinary negligence is a sufficient mens rea and the law falls within the city's delegated authority.

name: WILSON, J.
description: Concurred, but wrote separately to highlight that the basis for the City's authority to criminalize traffic infractions is unclear and that the question of whether cities can criminalize violations designated as traffic infractions by the state remains unresolved.

name: Chief Judge DiFIORE
description: Concurred, argued that eavesdropping warrants are executed where law enforcement intentionally records or overhears communications, not where the target or device is located, and that this interpretation is consistent with statutory language and legislative intent, ensuring centralized oversight and protecting privacy.

name: WILSON, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the statute does not authorize a New York court to issue a warrant for calls between non-residents not present in New York, and that the majority's interpretation grants law enforcement an unreasonable, unlimited geographic reach, infringing on privacy.

name: RIVERA, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the construction of snowmobile trails requiring the cutting and removal of thousands of trees and altering the wild forest violates the "forever wild" constitutional provision, necessitating a constitutional amendment.

name: STEIN, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the project does not constitute a "substantial change" to the Forest Preserve, as it balances protection with year-round public access and the timber cut is not substantial enough to impair its wild forest nature.

name: WILSON, J.
description: Concurred, argued that a search warrant for "entire premises" does not implicitly authorize the search of vehicles on the property without specific mention and probable cause for the vehicles themselves, upholding New York's stricter constitutional standards.

name: FEINMAN, J.
description: Dissented, argued that a valid warrant for "entire premises" should permit the search of vehicles parked on the premises if they could contain the items sought, viewing vehicles as containers and aligning with federal and other state court interpretations.

name: DiFIORE, C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority's decision deviates from federal and other state court interpretations regarding premises warrants and vehicle searches.

name: GARCIA, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority's decision deviates from federal and other state court interpretations regarding premises warrants and vehicle searches.
